title: Estimating Disaster Impact with contextual Pre and Post Disaster Datasets
html:
Computers can be used to model the impact and damage of potential disasters. The Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS) can leverage pre-event data and combine it with the event details to estimate the scale of a possible disaster, such as an earthquake. For example, if an earthquake is registered near the coast of Indonesia, GDACS can combine pre-crisis data sources, such as the population count, with event data (magnitude and depth) to determine the likely severity. Tsunami probabilities can also be determined and factored into the estimate. Such solutions are great for rapid alerting of a possible emergency.

But even if we know that there is an emergency to respond to, and its potential magnitude, we do not necessarily know where to respond. Within the emergency zone, there will be areas that are harder hit than others. We need to know the specific areas that might be terribly affected versus the areas that might not be so badly affected. The media and people on the ground can help guide us to a degree in the direct aftermath of a sudden onset emergency. However, in the case of Typhoon Haiyan last year, the CNN-effect drove most people to Tacloban even though there were other heavily affected areas.

So, how can we get a picture in the first day or two of an emergency that would tell us where things might be bad? How can we better focus our assessment teams and even relief teams based on data we get access to in the hours following an emergency? Effective targeting in the early hours and days is critical to life saving efforts.

One approach landed quietly in my inbox when I was responding to Typhoon Haiyan last year. Miguel Antonio Garcia, of the Barcelona Graduate School of Economics and now University of Zurich, compiled a composite index using pre- and post-crisis data and shared it with Luis Hernando Aguilar Ramírez (who was working with me) in a Google Spreadsheet. How was it different than the computer models? Miguel had selected relevant, available pre-crisis datasets (e.g. poverty incidence, population density, house size, etc) and combined it with post-event contextual data (e.g. storm surge height). It was something that almost anyone could compile. It did not require a machine or advanced algorithms.

In my sleep-deprived state, I didn’t understand right away what I was looking at. I just saw rows and columns of unprocessed data. Thankfully, Ivan Gayton of Médecins Sans Frontières was in the room and he quickly recognized what he could do with the data. He created several maps of the indicators [PDF] and we printed them onto one large poster. That set off a chain reaction as senior staff started studying the maps and asking more informed questions.

Nigel Woof and the MapAction team were able to add this impact estimate layer onto other maps [PDF], including Operational Presence maps. The combined “impact estimate-operational presence” maps were used that same evening at a key inter-cluster strategy meeting in Tacloban chaired by the Deputy Humanitarian Community (DHC). Immediately after this meeting, the DHC remarked to Nigel that these maps were invaluable in getting the key actors to at least start thinking spatially about the response. So not only did it let us ask more informed questions, but it really helped to give operational decision makers a better understanding of the situation in front of them.

These events happened in the second week of the response to Typhoon Haiyan and thus had no impact in the critical first days. However, it did get me thinking about how we could enable future responders to build such indexes in the early hours of any disaster.

Over the past few months, I was joined by Giedrius Kaveckis to study the approach, write simple guidance and develop a simple tool. We wanted something that could be easily customized to fit any situation and we needed it to work in any size of emergency.

Giedrius has done exactly that by providing a simple guidance document [PDF], suggested indicators by disaster type [PDF], and a Google Spreadsheet template [XLS] tool. These three items are part of a package to enable the creation of a “Sudden Onset Disaster Impact Severity Estimate Index” in any emergency.

We hope that the approach and the tool are simple enough that any information management officer, in any scale of emergency, can customize it to their needs and use it to help inform the assessment and response teams in the critical hours and days after a new emergency.  Sometimes it really is the simple things that can make the biggest difference.

The materials are open and free to use and/or customize as you need.  If you have any feedback or want to build improved versions, please do be in touch.

Andrej

Update: I was informed after posting that the data put together by Miguel was also used by Dwynn Trazo at the time to create a nice infographic comparing the the various affected regions in the Philippines.
teaser: A composite index of pre-disaster and post-event data offered an alternative to computer models for estimating disaster impact in the Philippines.
seo_description: How Miguel's composite index combined datasets such as poverty and population density with storm surge data to estimate disaster impact.
